On the one hand we have a press dispatch of the 4th of January to the effect that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had said that Canada is willing to increase trade with the U.S.S.R. in a limited list of commodities. On the other hand, we have the attitude displayed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs which is certainly not to the effect that there should be an expansion of trade.
The ambassador from the U.S.S.R. said some three weeks ago: "Don't worry about details at the moment; the main thing is to start trading". Certainly all of us hope for the day when trade will be universal, but do we not have to consider whether or not almost everything which we would supply would be strategic materials in the world of today when nations as a whole, not armies, are on the offensive in the war of ideas? The U.S.S.R. is taking textiles from France, selling iron and manganese to Britain, buying ships from West Germany, and has started to trade

with Greece, Denmark and Norway. Australia is importing Russian canned salmon and crabmeat.
There should be an enunciation by the government of Canada's policy regarding trade with the U.S.S.R., which is not so important materially if we are to judge by the trade of the past but certainly important in that consideration must be given at all times to the fact that if we supply them what they require as directed by the state we shall indeed be playing into their hands.
I ask the minister to say whether in his opinion the expansion of trade would consolidate the Malenkov regime. Which course are we to follow? Is he in a position to say whether, in the opinion of the officials of his department and of himself, this newly acquired desire of the U.S.S.R. is a bona fide desire to expand world trade or is designed to divide the free world, eventually to dominate it and finally to destroy it?
Can the minister give any assurance that if Canada or other NATO countries enter into expanded trade with Russia we will have assurance from the U.S.S.R. that those countries in Europe contiguous to it and friendly to us will not be subjected in the days ahead to the well known practice of the U.S.S.R. in the late twenties and early thirties of dumping excess goods on European markets, thereby destroying our markets and also our trade in various countries?
In Britain the federation of British industries has gone into this matter in considerable detail, and apparently the investigations have been made with the blessing of the United Kingdom government. I am not going to read the entire release issued by the United Kingdom information office on the 14th of January last, but I will read a few excerpts which I think particularly embody the general conclusions arrived at. The report contains the following:
. . . there is, in our opinion, no ground for thinking that east-west trade, including trade with China, can in the foreseeable future account for more than a comparatively modest proportion of the United Kingdom's total volume of trade. . . It is our view that, largely owing to the Korean war and the intensification of the strategic controls, enterprise has been discouraged and a feeling engendered that there is something wrong and unpatriotic about east-west trade, even in those items excluded by the embargoes. This is emphatically a feeling to be dispelled.
I am giving both sides at the moment. After viewing contentions on both sides of the argument, the conclusions are summarized in these words:
(i)	that trade with countries of the eastern bloc is likely permanently to offer fewer opportunities than before the war, and that trade with China has
External Affairs
only modest scope for expansion on account of her limited capacity as an exporter and earner of sterling coupled with the reduced market for Chinese exports;
(ii)	that such opportunities of east-west trade as exist in non-strategic goods should, nevertheless, be pursued without any inhibitions arising from political considerations;
(iii)	that members of the federation in their dealings with Russia, countries of the eastern bloc, and China, should avoid channels which are likely to turn matters of commerce pure and simple to account for the purposes of communist political propaganda.
I feel the Canadian people have a right to know the attitude to be taken by the Canadian government on this important matter. Certainly the trade existent now is of no consequence. According to a recent Canadian Press dispatch, in the first ten months of 1953 we exported $406 worth of goods to the U.S.S.R. and we imported $416,000 worth, mostly furs. What is the U.S.SR. prepared to ship us? What has she available? Is it a fact that about the only products of which she has a surplus are oil, coal and timber, in respect of which we in Canada are looking for markets?
However that may be, Canadian people in industry, agriculture and labour are looking for a statement by the government on its stand in this matter. Certainly if trade is to be expanded the definition of non-strategic materials will have to be drawn with greater care.
In conclusion, I would say that we in the opposition intend in the days ahead to follow the course which has been ours throughout the years. We intend to endeavour to secure, in our external relations, a unity of purpose, a degree of uniform policy, so that in our relationships with the countries of the world we shall be able to discharge our responsibilities in the days ahead with firm and abiding purpose and with good will to all nations who will reciprocate.
Mr. M. J. Cold we 11 (Roseiown-Biggar): I
should first like to associate myself, Mr. Speaker, both with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and with the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), in expressing the regret we all feel that Gordon Graydon was removed from us and can no longer participate in the work of this very important department. I should like to associate myself also with what the minister said about the late Hume Wrong. Like many of those in the house I have known him for a number of years and appreciate the remarkable work he did for Canada in those days when, with the minister and a group of young men brought into the department very largely by the late Mr. O. D. Skelton, the policy

External Affairs
was pursued of building up Canada's Department of External Affairs and giving us recognition throughout the world as a selfgoverning nation.
I should like also to say something about Mr. Patterson, such a delightful personality. Some hon. members sitting here this afternoon had the opportunity of being associated with him at the United Nations this autumn. It came as a great shock to us to learn that, going for a week end holiday to his residence in Boston, shortly after his arrival there he died. He was a fine, Christian gentleman, with whom many of us were happy to be associated at the United Nations.
This afternoon the minister said there was unanimity in this house on the fundamental principles underlying the policies of his department. That is true. Those fundamental principles, I take it, are the principles of security and peace. But having agreed on the principles, there is plenty of room for disagreement on those aspects that many of us think should be the policies by which both security and peace may be attained.
This afternoon I shall say some things in connection with our external affairs that are said in common with progressive and anti-communist movements and parties all across the world, not only in our own commonwealth but in the Far East and in the countries of western Europe. Let no one say that because some of the communist parties have picked up some of these policies from the progressive democratic socialist parties of the world, anything I may say in this house is communist propaganda.
The debate on external affairs can, as usual, I think serve a very useful purpose at this time because it gives the minister an opportunity of discussing our relations with other countries. It gives an opportunity to members of the house to express some views concerning recent developments in the world situation, developments I may say both diplomatically and militarily. Of course these are inseparable, for if diplomatic relations improve it should be possible to reduce our vast expenditures on various phases of rearmament.
On May 5 last, as the minister said, the last extended debate on external affairs took place in this house. I remarked then that there seemed to have been a sharp change, both in Russian propaganda and in Russian tactics, in the short nine or ten weeks that had followed since the death of Joseph Stalin. I think it is generally agreed throughout the world that, in the last 11 months or so since that event, startling changes have occurred in the Soviet union. Whatever we may think are the reasons

for these changes, and perhaps for events like the liquidation of Beria and his immediate associates, there has been an easing of tension in the world since the death of Stalin.
I think that as a rule mankind has breathed a sigh of relief, and countless millions pray that, however slow the process, we may be able to move toward an era in which, little by little and bit by bit, the outstanding problems between the powerful nations will be settled not by force of arms, not by making threats against one another, but by intelligent negotiation.
Within Russia, as the minister said this afternoon, there have been changes-great changes-in the economic outlook of the new government. And I say to my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other members of the house that I believe one of the means of achieving peaceful understanding, of achieving peace by negotiation, is to do whatever we can to encourage trade between the nations.
Now, do not misunderstand me. I do not believe we should supply a potential aggressor with strategic materials, but I do believe that the visits of British businessmen, a large number of whom we are told are over there at the moment, or of businessmen from any of the western countries of the world, can do no less than bring about some better understanding on both sides of the iron curtain.
To contemplate war, with the frightful weapons now at hand, is I believe to contemplate universal catastrophe. Because of the dire threat which has overhung the world in recent years, nations equally fearful of such a struggle may find ways and means of resolving outstanding problems and difficulties by intelligent approach and by negotiation. And I say that the gestures made by the Russians at this time, paralleled by gestures made by the President of the United States, and certainly paralleled by several statements made recently by Sir Winston Churchill, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, all taken together have given great hope to the world that we may be entering upon an era, perhaps very much prolonged but nevertheless productive of peaceful negotiations and ultimate understanding among the nations of the world.
I think it is wrong for any of us, at a time when there are possibilities of such understanding and negotiation, to use language or threats which may make negotiation and understanding still more difficult. In saying this I am not minimizing the dangers that exist. But those dangers of course are apparent to most of our people; and I believe

they are quite apparent to most of the statesmen who have the responsibility for maintaining the security of their own countries and for promoting the peace of the world.
In the last ten months, as I have said, important changes have occurred in the attitude of Soviet leaders. Again, whether this is a new tactic or not-and these approaches may well be a new tactic-we should be prepared to welcome any such change in attitude; and at the same time we should retain the strong position we have attained. In retaining that strong position we should not, however, lose any opportunity to reach agreement on such issues, however minor they may be, as become possible of settlement through negotiation.
Let us remember that until very recently Russian leaders have said nothing that could be construed as being friendly to any of the democratic powers. Sometimes their references have been designedly insulting, making co-operation virtually impossible. And those of us who have been at the United Nations from time to time know how true that statement is. But I should say at once that leading statesmen in the democratic nations, and particularly in the United States, have at almost every opportunity denounced Russian leaders and the Soviet union in almost equally unmeasured terms.
It is I think regrettable that whenever proposals have been made by either side for co-operation, newspapers in Russia and in the United States, as well as in our own and other countries, have jumped to the conclusion immediately, depending upon which side made the proposal, of course, that such proposal should be denounced, thus making negotiation almost impossible. In Russia, the organ of the Soviet union, Pravda, has been guilty time and time again. And while that organ of the Soviet union has been more restrained recently, many leading newspapers in the United States have continued to pursue a policy which could have no other effect than to prejudice the possibility of peaceful negotiation. I think that was particularly true as we approached the meeting of the foreign ministers at Berlin. Believing as we do in a free press, we also believe that it should be a responsible press, rather than one unnecessarily provocative in its criticism, particularly concerning pending negotiations among the great powers.
Those of us who were at the United Nations last autumn shared, I think, the view that was very generally held there, that world tension had decreased somewhat. The minister himself said that this was so this afternoon. There were still evidences of truculence on the part of some of the great powers, notably on
External Affairs
the part of the United States and the Soviet union. But there was less bitterness in debate, and a desire on the part of most of the nations represented there to arrive at solutions of some of the outstanding problems.
I should like to say that in my opinion the United Nations has been and is the greatest barrier we now have against the outbreak of war. Many minor disputes have been settled through United Nations agencies, and the forum provided for the great powers has undoubtedly prevented the outbreak of war on a world-wide scale. Certainly it has prevented the outbreak of war among some of the minor nations. In other words, in the sharp issues which have arisen in the Far East and in Europe as well as elsewhere, the United Nations has provided a forum for discussion, and to that extent has stood as a barrier against the outbreak of war.
I want to say how disturbed I have been during the past few days to see that one of our departments of education, that in the province of British Columbia, has withdrawn from circulation among the schools the United Nations association monthly bulletin. The bulletin, which has been circulated in all the provinces, including British Columbia, is now being withdrawn, according to a statement emanating from Victoria. I wonder what is happening in that province when I read in the press that the mayor of Victoria and some of his associates are actually suggesting the burning of books they dislike. I wonder how far in the direction of totalitarianism we are moving in this country when we see that kind of thing in a province like British Columbia.
I would like to see the bulletin of the United Nations association more widely read. It cannot be called a communist organization, you know, because it is headed by General Burns, whom we all know favourably in this city. We believe that while, in view of the world situation in recent years, it has been necessary to enter into arrangements for mutual defence, such as those envisaged in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, it is equally important to use every means within our power to promote the economic and social well-being of people everywhere; and again, may I say, through the United Nations agencies, and through our own Colombo plan to supplement those agencies.
In that field we believe too little has been done. When the North Atlantic Treaty Organization was established we in this party urged our government to suggest an article committing the signatories to mutual economic aid for their general welfare. Thus article 2 of the treaty became one of the most important considerations which led us to support NATO. And at every opportunity we have

External Affairs
criticized the organization because it has failed to implement that article in the manner in which we feel it should have been implemented. I say to the government that at the present time they should be more insistent on the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We believe that the policy of confining aid within the organization to military aid, which has largely been done, is not only wrong but may ultimately defeat the very objective of the treaty itself.
The difficulties arising in France and in Italy, to mention two of the NATO nations, are due to the economic conditions of the people within those nations; and, particularly in the case of France, the vast military expenditures on rearmament and on the operations in Indo-China, which apparently France herself is very anxious to bring to an end by negotiation. The economic situation in those NATO associates of ours, if not relieved, may lead to the breakdown of the whole anticommunist front among the democratic powers. Therefore once again I urge our government to give leadership, both within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the United Nations, for greater emphasis in the economic field.
We believe that with the easing of tension and the achieving of our rearmament targets we are in a position where we can reduce our expenditures for military defence and use the relief obtained not for the reduction of income and other taxes within Canada, but to a large extent at least for the giving of more economic aid under the United Nations' technical assistance program and the Colombo plan.
Let me add that I believe Canada has a unique opportunity of giving such leadership at the present time. In saying what I am about to say I want to have it differentiated from anything in relation to trying to make trade out of the Prime Minister's departure on his tour. The Prime Minister is about to leave on a good-will tour around the world. I said earlier this afternoon that I hoped that he would act as an ambassador of good will on behalf of the Canadian people. What I said earlier I should like to repeat on behalf of my colleagues and myself. We wish him a safe, pleasant and productive journey.
I am sure that he will realize that in conveying messages of good will in the countries he visits he will be conveying the sentiments of all the Canadian people. But I am going to suggest this, that he might demonstrate our good will in a very practical way. At the moment we have vast quantities of food available to a hungry world if they

had the means to purchase it. Besides this we have, for example, at least one industry in which there is considerable unemployment, but which is equipped to produce machines for the production of food in large quantity. I am not suggesting that we sell anything; I am suggesting that we give something.
On December 26 last the London Economist, which is one of the foremost papers of its kind in the world, published a report on conditions in southeast Asia. This authoritative newspaper pointed out that as a result of the cessation of hostilities in Korea and the easing of world tension, countries in southeast Asia were facing a situation which to say the least is most discouraging. The fall of prices for their products and the maintenance of high prices for capital and other equipment they need from abroad will, the Economist says, necessarily interfere with the achievement of the standards of living originally planned when, for example, the Colombo plan was adopted. The Economist says that one of two things must be done, and I am going to quote the exact words as they appeared in the paper:
There must either be greater temporary sacrifice on the part of the people themselves . . .
And heaven knows how much more sacrifice the undernourished, underfed, underprivileged people of India, Pakistan, Ceylon and the other Far Eastern countries can undergo. I continue:
... or there must be an increase in the amount of external aid which in any case has never been guaranteed as adequate to close the gap between intention and availability.
Our suggestion to the Prime Minister is that, in view of the circumstances and the need to raise the standards of living, if we are to offset communist propaganda in those areas he make the generous offer of gifts of food, particularly perhaps wheat of which we have a large quantity, and instruments of production such as farm machinery, to the governments of those countries. Those gifts- I emphasize "gifts"-would be in addition to the Colombo plan, and regarded as part of our defence budget, and marketed by the governments of the receiving countries so the proceeds could be used in carrying forward projects designed to increase their own production and raise their standards of living.
This would not have the effect of dumping goods across the world. We believe that it would not have the effect of depressing the prices of those commodities on the world market. Why? Because the recipient countries are not in a position to purchase those supplies abroad, their external purchasing power having been reduced by the drastic fall in

prices of their exports. It is not a question of replacing something they may buy from abroad, but something we might be able to give them and which they have not the means to buy abroad.
Let me say that when I suggest a reduction should be made in our expenditures on armaments, I am merely reiterating the opinion which seems to have been expressed and has been interpreted by the newspapers as having been expressed by Lord Alexander, the Minister of Defence in the United Kingdom, who is reported by the newspapers yesterday as announcing that a plan is to be introduced which:
. . . seeks to keep Britain's defence expenditure, now more than 40 per cent of the budget or about $98 a person annually, within control.
The New York Times service, quoted by the Montreal Gazette, says this of the minister's statement:
The new plan was interpreted by sources close to the government as a reflection of its belief that the immediate danger of war with the Soviet union has receded steadily in the last year and that time has come to re-plan defence in anticipation of a considerable period of uneasy balance between east and west.	!
And when we remember that President Eisenhower in his message to congress quite recently suggested a 10 per cent cut in expenditures on armaments of that country, and when according to this morning's paper the Department of National Defence of Canada is to cut the defence expenditure recommended to this parliament by more than 5 per cent, I think it underlines what I have just been saying. But it seems to me that the fact the United States can cut its expenditures by 10 per cent indicates that we should be able to cut ours probably by about the same amount, and 10 per cent of $2 billion used for economic aid in the countries where communist propaganda is prevalent and effective because of the distress conditions, poverty, misery and want that exist there, would be one of the best means of defence on behalf of the democratic nations that we could find; and I make that suggestion. I say we believe that Canada should whenever possible give a lead in promoting policies that will lead to the removal of fear of war and the deliverance of mankind from the ever-present fear of starvation and want which afflict millions of people all across the world.
Last spring President Eisenhower, both in his fireside talk in April and in his message to congress on May 5, proposed a program which met with acclaim everywhere in the world. For the first time it was proposed by the President of the United States that greater 83276-102
External Affairs
emphasis should be placed upon development of technical aid and assistance to backward areas, particularly in Asia.
Since then I am sorry to say-and my experience at the United Nations and my observation of the policy of the United States delegation lead me to think that this is so- there has been in the United States a reversion to the previous emphasis on military preparedness and the securing of bases far beyond the borders of that country. A few days ago I noted that the president of Turkey declared that his country would welcome economic aid rather than more military equipment and supplies.
Then the rumours that the United States was seeking an agreement with Pakistan for bases and the supply of armaments caused great alarm in India as well as, may I say, among the peoples and governments associated with our democratic cause. Peaceful negotiations are made more difficult when rumours of this kind go mainly or partly uncontradicted. The alarm in India was widespread and expressed by Prime Minister Nehru in no uncertain terms. Anything which drives India away from the association she now has with the West is not only dangerous but in my opinion may be disastrous to the world.
I agree with the minister and with the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who both recognized the importance of having with us the countless millions of people who are in southeast Asia. If we lose them we have lost the bulk of the world's manhood and womanhood to the Soviet union. So I say that the proposal for the United States to take bases in Pakistan and to arm Pakistan is a suicidal policy on the part of the United States, and is equally suicidal for those of us who are associated with the United States in the democratic cause.
I say that negotiations are made more difficult with the Soviet union by such reports because to them at least they are indications of aggressive feelings on the part of the leading power among the democracies. I wonder what we would think if the Soviet union suggested to Mexico that she should establish bases in that country. I wonder what we would say if the Soviet union requested also to establish bases in Cuba or in other places and islands around us. I wonder what we would say, and I wonder how we could feel that negotiations proposed under those circumstances were sincere. I say that every effort should be made to prevent a policy of the description I have just mentioned being put into effect. Our government should take

External Affairs
a leading part as a member of the commonwealth, as a member of the United Nations and as a close neighbour and friend of the United States, in advising the United States against such a policy whenever an opportunity occurs.
I want to say something about the release of prisoners in Korea. The minister said they had been released as civilians. The manner in which the press has treated these releases certainly has caused considerable concern to a good many people. I do not propose to discuss the protracted negotiations which failed to reach agreement concerning this matter. We know that dealing with the communists is difficult, but we also know that Canada and some other nations believed that the inclusion of India in the proposed peace conference was desirable, and that if India had been admitted it is possible the conference might have been held. We voted that way, but the United States was able to muster sufficient votes among its South American friends to prevent the two-thirds majority required for the inclusion of India, so India was left out.
We have been told that the North Koreans and Chinese communists who refused to return to their countries have been liberated, but if we can believe the press stories it is a rather strange kind of liberation. It puts the North Koreans who refused to return to North Korea in lorries and transfers them to South Korean camps for screening, and ships Chinese who refused to go back to China to Formosa for similar screening. This appears to be a method of conscription which left no opportunity to the former prisoners of war to become civilians. One is bound to ask if Canada agreed to this method of liberation. In view of this episode is it any wonder that the Chinese and the North Koreans fear that the proposed peace negotiations may be but the prelude to an attack by Syngman Rhee and Chiang Kai-shek on China proper?
These are matters which cause grave misgivings among those of us who are anxious to see peace and understanding promoted among the nations.
Then look at Berlin. At the present time the foreign ministers of the United States, the United Kingdom, France and the Soviet union are meeting in Berlin. We all hope that at least some success will be attained there, but again prior to the meeting powerful voices in the United States and large sections of the press were bitterly denouncing the calling of the conference and dooming it to failure. This, it should be said, was in the sharpest possible contrast to statements made by public men in the United Kingdom

and France, where the opinions expressed were so different from those expressed by powerful and loud voices in the United States, and by sections of the press.
I say this as a friend of the United States because I think there are groups of people in that country who are making it difficult for the democratic powers to achieve their objectives in ironing out some of the difficulties existing in the world that may lead to war. It seems to us that in dealing with a nation which does not believe that the press and speech in the democracies are both free, comments made on forthcoming conferences should be thoroughly responsible.
We believe that Germany today represents what may become a festering sore in the very heart of Europe. As long as the country is divided into two sections there is little hope of building a Germany which can co-operate in promoting the peace and progress of the world. In our opinion the longer she is divided the more likely it is that former nazis in West Germany will regain much of their influence over the West German people and, on the other hand, that the communist leaders in East Germany will be more firmly entrenched, making unity of the country and peace in Europe still more difficult to achieve. May I say that I thoroughly agree that any unification of Germany, as was suggested by the minister in his speech this afternoon, cannot be a unification of two governments, or a government set up from those two governments. It can only be a unification if it is preceded by free elections held under the supervision of the United Nations. Certainly proposals for the rearmament of West Germany before unification would in our opinion-and let there be no misunderstanding; we are not following the communist line when we say this, we are expressing the views of the great socialist and labour movement in Europe and across the world-have a disastrous effect on hopes for the peaceful development of the European community.
One can understand the attitude of France, and the hesitation she has in joining EDC, because not twice but three times during the last hundred years she has been invaded by German armies, causing not only great suffering but terrible losses of life and property. On the other hand, we recognize that the western nations cannot assume all the responsibility for the defence of Germany should aggression occur. Indeed, the very rejuvenation of Germany-the very fact that her industries are now able to export vast quantities of goods, that she has been able to build homes for her people and that she

has been able to put new and modern machinery in her factories-is due to the fact that none of her men have been taken out of production and put into the armed forces, that none of her industries have been engaged in the manufacture of war materials and that none of her finances have been used for military purposes which, while necessary, are wasteful.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: She has to make a large contribution to the occupation costs.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Yes; she has to make
large contributions to the occupation costs, but even those have not been comparable to what France and the United Kingdom have been paying in their rearmament programs and in the maintenance of armies, involving loss of productive manpower, to support NATO and prevent aggression in the world.
As I say, we recognize immediately that the western nations cannot be expected to assume all the responsibility for the defence of Germany should aggression occur. Consequently, while opposed to the rearmament of Germany, we believe that after unification a disarmed, united Germany might have her neutrality guaranteed by the United Nations and particularly-by an agreement among the powers-by Russia and the western powers. But that agreement is some distance off, at least.
In our opinion, however, whatever is done to integrate German manpower into a western European defence system-and that may be necessary-neither the German armament industry nor German leadership should be permitted to revive once again the military aspirations of a new Germany. That, it seems to us, must be prevented by every possible means. Certainly we should not agree at all to any likelihood of a German army, under German command, with the old officers of the nazi regime; and what is more important, I suppose, in a way, is that the non-commissioned officers who are in close contact with the men should be carefully screened to see that they were not supporters of the old nazi regime. Any such troops should be organized under non-German military commanders and non-German staff.
This afternoon my friend the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) mentioned the point that the United States is contemplating withdrawal of her troops from Europe, in large part, and substituting new machines and new and devastating instruments of destruction as a means of defence. In his address to the general assembly of the United Nations, President Eisenhower clearly outlined the devastating effects that the use 83276-102J
External Affairs
of such weapons would involve. For example -and I am going to quote him directly-he said:
A single air group, whether afloat or land-based, can now deliver-
That is the weapons in the possession of the United States.
-on an available target, a destructive cargo (of bombs) exceeding the power of all bombs that fell on Britain in all of world war II.
That is, whether afloat or land-based, one group of planes could deliver a destructive cargo of bombs exceeding the power of all the bombs that fell on all of Britain in all of world war II. Of the United States stockpile of atomic weapons he said something else, and I quote again. He said that it-
*-exceeds by many times the explosive equivalent of the total of all bombs and all shells that came from every plane and every gun in every theatre of war through all the years of world war II.
Then President Eisenhower went on to say that the United States had no monopoly of this great power, and that while he believed in American superiority in numbers of such weapons, the facts are that the Soviet union has a growing stockpile too. He then made a proposal which I believe every human being must welcome, namely that this great destructive force can and should be developed for the benefit of all mankind. He therefore proposed that the governments principally involved-and he qualified it by "to the extent permitted by elementary prudence", and I think he was right in doing that-as he put it, should begin now and continue to make, from their stockpiles of normal uranium and fissionable materials, joint contributions to an international atomic energy agency set up under the aegis of the United Nations. This agency, he went on to say, would be charged not only with the responsibility for the storage and protection of the contributed materials, but would mobilize international experts to develop and apply atomic energy for the peaceful purposes of the world.
This, of course, I may say, is a departure, and a fundamental one, from the proposals made from time to time before the atomic energy commission of the United Nations and, in my opinion, if agreement could be reached it would represent a great step forward in the peaceful development of this great new source of energy.
As Mr. Churchill said a short time ago, the very terror of these weapons to which the President referred might be something of an insurance against their use in war; but the important thing is not only, as some suggest, to outlaw the use of such weapons

External Affairs
*-and the outlawing of such weapons, of course, may be quite problematical if a nation is faced with defeat in war-but to find ways and means of banishing war and the threat of war. That is the only insurance against war.
I repeat that in our opinion this cannot be done by threats of the use of force; nor by the building up of armies, navies and air forces, though under certain circumstances they may be necessary; nor by securing bases here and there all across the world and filling them with devastating weapons of war. In our opinion this can only be done by negotiation among the great powers and by rapidly raising the standards of living everywhere in the world. I want to emphasize again that to my mind, in the ultimate, that is the best defence that democracy has; I refer to the raising of standards of living of the underprivileged in the undeveloped areas of the world.
The foreign ministers in Berlin . are reported to be likely to discuss not only the matter of atomic weapons and the Russian proposal for outlawing them but the wider problem of disarmament. I know something of the difficulties they will face, because I was present at the United Nations in 1946 when our own Prime Minister, then our minister of external affairs, foreshadowed the organization of the Atlantic community for the first time because of the failure of the great powers to do anything in implementing that chapter of the charter which called for negotiations among their military staffs. When, at the conclusion of that assembly, disarmament was proposed, we saw the brushing aside of that proposal by Mr. Molotov and the gestures made by Sir Hartley Shawcross at the same time to the effect that Britain was prepared to give to the United Nations the keys to her factories, the right to pull up the blinds and see exactly what they were doing in order that everyone might understand the problem and come to some arrangement with regard to disarmament.
Russian proposals in the past have been unacceptable but perchance under the new regime-and I say "perchance"-more satisfactory proposals to the world might come and might be considered. We might make more satisfactory proposals also.

it never will be done. I do not believe in that kind of thing. I do not believe, either, that as individuals or as a government we should take such an attitude.

speechtext:
My hon. friend says that it will never be done by the socialists. Let me tell him that the great act of statesmanship that brought India into the world as a nation and kept her on our side was undertaken by a socialist government. I just want to tell my hon. friend that. In any event, it is our hope that Canada will use her influence, whenever it is possible to do so, to secure the widest possible measures of disarmament.
I must conclude, because my time is nearly up. There are many other problems that could have been discussed, some of which arose at the United Nations last autumn. I hope that some of my colleagues will address themselves to some of these problems. Suffice it to say that on several occasions I wished that Canada had taken a stronger attitude regarding some of the problems before the United Nations last autumn. To mention one or two of them, there are the situations in Morocco and Tunis and the threats to human freedom in the Union of South Africa.
I think those are matters which affect not only the welfare of masses of humanity but, in the ultimate, the peace of the world. I should like to see Canada give more leadership in endeavouring to solve these problems than we have seemed inclined to give.
I want to say to the minister and the government that I appreciate the opportunity that has been afforded by setting aside this day to discuss some of these problems. I have tried to place before the house views which may not be generally shared by all hon. members, but which nonetheless are shared by millions of people throughout the world who are not communists, and I believe they are worthy of consideration.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also feel that I should express appreciation to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) for making it possible for us to discuss today these very important matters relating to external affairs. I listened with a great deal of interest to what the minister called his general and discursive survey of world affairs. I enjoyed it. He took us on another of the tours on which he so often takes us, and while he did not get clear around the world this time

at least he gave us a glimpse of what is behind the curtain of time, perhaps more than anything else, and that we do appreciate.
I want to say at once that we join with him in mourning the passing of two great Canadian servants, Mr. Hume Wrong and Mr. Patterson. The minister's department is going to suffer as a consequence of the passing of these men who in the past proved themselves to be most capable servants and made great contributions to the favourable relationships that Canada now enjoys with other countries.
I missed today the good-humoured and well-reasoned speech usually delivered by the late hon. member for Peel, who was the spokesman for the Conservative party. But I think on this very first occasion the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has demonstrated that he is a worthy successor. Many of the things he brought before us today proved not only interesting but challenging, and I shall have something to say about a few of his comments before I am finished.
I think I would perhaps be neglecting my duty if I did not make brief comment on such important things as the question of German rearmament, NATO, and so on. Without going over all the arguments, or even introducing any further argument, I should say right away that I do not see how in the world the western world is going to be able to meet the challenge of the communist areas unless Germany is made capable of taking a very important part in her own defence and the defence of western Europe. Much as I have feared the rearmament of Germany and have wished that it could be otherwise, I do not see any other answer to the security of western Europe than to rearm Germany, take her into the European defence community, if that is possible, and see to it as far as we can that a rearmed Germany is never able to use her new-found or refound strength for aggressive purposes.
I think we also have to rebuild Austria. I believe it was a mistake in the first place to dismember the Austro-Hungarian empire, and I think the world is beginning to understand that that is so. We feel the need of Austria today and of her steadfastness and great ability in the western concert of nations.
As I listened to the minister this afternoon I wondered, as perhaps many other hon. members did, what is being done about those ethnic groups behind the iron curtain who all during the years have been opposed to totalitarianism in any form, who have been the champions of liberty, but are now held captive by the U.S.S.R. and her satellites. I wondered if anything had been done to make
External Affairs
it possible for them to make their contribution because, after all, I think one of the greatest contributions to the downfall of imperialist communism throughout the world is going to be the work of those ethnic groups who still love their freedom and are determined to regain it. I suppose the minister could have said something about that, but naturally he could not cover the whole orbit today.
Although I have little criticism to make of the minister's speech and find little wrong with it, he did leave me without an answer to a number of important questions, questions that almost every thinking person must be asking himself at this time. The first of these would be: Has the United Nations effort in Korea served even slightly to insulate the world against a third global war, or has it served to bring such a conflict nearer? Maybe he cannot answer that. That may be an assignment that no person could possibly carry out today. But it is something that many people are asking, and I think with good reason.
A second question: Have we learned anything of real value to the human race as a consequence of the billions of dollars of material wealth spent and the many thousands of gallant lives lost in the Korean conflict? If so, what is it that we have learned and how can we make use of these lessons in the future?
A third question:	Who has thus far come
off victor in Korea, and why? Fourth: What hope is there that a Korean peace treaty will be agreed upon and signed? In the long negotiations ahead on that particular matter, how far will the United Nations go in yielding to communist demands and what effect will those concessions have, if they are made, in strengthening the communist part of the world and weakening the free part?
These are matters of grave concern to me because, after all, mankind today needs guideposts and iron rods to which to hold. It seems to me that if we realize anything at all we must realize that the objective of communist imperialism is to become boss of the world by any means that is available. Consequently anything that strengthens the communist part of the world will weaken our part of the world by just that much.
Our guide in determining our position on any important question, it seems to me, should be what position can we take that will strengthen the free world and contribute to the weakening of communist imperialism? We in the free nations have been blind to that guide for many years. Certainly we have not kept it clearly before us in the negotiations that have taken place or in the

External Affairs
development of our policies. The tragic result of that neglect has been a constantly expanding and growing communist menace to the freedom, happiness and security of the world. The western nations have been too ready to grant concessions. Many of our leading men have allowed themselves to be blinded to the realities of the situation, perhaps in a measure because they have allowed their advisory councils to be packed with unfaithful, subversive people who have been guilty of perfidy and treason on some occasions.
The fifth question that is in my mind is this. What are we working for as a nation? By that I mean what is the real objective of our Canadian foreign policy? What do we want to achieve-let us give ourselves a reasonable time-say in the next 20 years? I should think that a clear-cut and forthright answer to that question alone would be refreshing, and might serve to arouse hope and faith in the Canadian people. In my judgment there was never a time when hope and faith so needed to be aroused as it does today. This, and perhaps a good many other vital questions, the minister left unanswered in his speech. I realize that, as an excuse, it can be said he did not have time to deal with everything. We did not expect him to do that. Perhaps in the course of rebuttal, if lie gives any, or in the near future he may Tie able to deal with some of these very important matters.
' Even the things the minister did say today left us, at least some of us, with a feeling that we had not made very much progress over the years. Now, I hasten to pay the minister a compliment because I do not want him to think for one moment that I am saying what I have said just to be difficult and carping. Speaking to the Canadian public relations society in Montreal on January 5 of this year, the minister had this to say about foreign policy, and I quote his words as I received them in a report of his speech:
But in the long run, a foreign policy which has a sound moral basis will prevail over one which has not, providing we build on that base a structure of strength with freedom.
I was struck with those words, and I want to deal with them. If that is the wellspring from which our whole external policy arises, then I must admit it gives me some feeling of confidence and hope for the future. I do not think we can go very far wrong if we make absolutely certain that we do build our foreign policy on a moral basis, and one of strength and freedom. It is against the background the minister outlined that we should attempt to measure Canada's foreign policy. I think we should dig into it and find out for ourselves whether, in fact, it has a

sound moral basis; whether we are, in reality, building on that moral basis a structure of strength with freedom. Perhaps we are; but if we are to know that, then the elements of our foreign policy will have to be much more clearly stated than we have heard them so far.
For almost 15 years now the world has been enveloped in war. For most of those years there has existed somewhere in the world armed conflict, which we called "hot war". For the last few years we have experienced a combination of "hot war", such as in Korea and Indo-China, and "cold war", which is the battle for men's minds in the ideological or psychological field over the whole world. People generally, I find, are yearning for peace. They are anxiously scanning every sign, every portent, to discover whether there is indeed any possibility for peace. Many people everywhere are inclined to hook on to any proposition which would seem to hold some possibility of peace in the near future. Right now it seems to be the fashion to suggest meetings with the Russians or with the Chinese or with some other communist group. Everyone seems, evidently, to think that if we can get down to a conference with the communists we can work out a basis for real peace. I have heard that for many months.
I was keenly interested, therefore, in an article which appeared in the January 29 issue of U.S. News and World Report. This article appears under the heading "Talk with the communists; 120 million words, little gain by us." I hasten to say that I have not checked these figures, and they may not be accurate. I think perhaps that even if they are proven inaccurate they do illustrate very well the point I wanted to make. There are some rather arresting facts produced in the article, which I think it might be well if hon. members would consider for just a moment.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the dinner hour I was about to place before the house some rather arresting facts that were contained in an article which appeared in the January 29 issue of U.S. News and World Report. I made it clear, sir, that I had not checked the figures in the article; but I did say that even allowing for a substantial margin of error in them, the article would illustrate the point I wanted to make, and illustrate it very well indeed.

I should like to take just a few minutes to place these facts and figures before the house, particularly as they relate to this feeling on the part of so many people throughout the world that if they could just get down to discussions, conferences with the communists, everything could be worked out very well, and that peace would be coming soon and easily. An analysis of this article shows that in the eight post-war years more than 120 million words have been spoken in formal official talks with the communists. There has been no time in the eight years when talks were not going on in some place or another with communist countries, and the one tangible result to date has been a truce in Korea, a truce that the communists considered a victory for themselves.
Out of all this experience one rather striking conclusion has been drawn, and it is this. Few words are required if the communists are getting what they want, but words in endless profusion are required to lead to any result if the communists are not getting what they want. It is amazing to note that just before the present meeting with the Russians over the question of Germany, 525,000 words were spoken in 50 hours of talks just in an effort to decide on the spot at which the big four conference would be held. And there was no result. The Americans, British and French then submitted an offer that appeared to be much closer to the Russian terms, and after only a few dozen words were spoken everything was settled in short order.
If we go back to Yalta, it is said that it took over 220,000 words of talk in just seven sessions of conference to give Russia dominance in vast areas of the world. At Potsdam only 408,000 words were spoken. On that occasion Russia got what she wanted in Germany, and as a consequence today something like 17 million Germans are slaves to the Russian machine in that part of Germany.
In contrast to this, in an effort to bring about an Austrian peace treaty we learn that 11,900,000 words have been spoken in 378 full-dress meetings over a period of eight years, and without any agreement nor, it seems to me, the possibility of any agreement so far as can be seen now. It appears that Russia has not yet managed to get what she wants in this case, and therefore she is going to go on talking, and continue to go on talking. When we speak of trying to obtain unity for Germany, which for some time now has been divided into the east and west zones, let us remember that there have
External Affairs
been 1,380 meetings at which 43,500,000 words have been spoken, but again with no result.
The reason appears to be that the Russian terms have not been met. I suppose if we were to soften up and make concessions, as we have done in some other places in the world, it would not take long to reach an agreement. The famous Korean negotiations involved, I am told, 575 formal meetings at which it is said that 18,100,000 words were spoken. And that does not tell us how much doodling was done in absolute silence, with one side glaring across at the other and perhaps saying nothing. These meetings were carried on over a period of nearly two years, without any progress. At the end of that time terms were fixed that apparently met the conditions laid down by the Chinese communists, and thereafter the truce came very quickly. Following the armistice, talks about peace in Korea went ahead for some time, but they have now broken down because the United States is not willing to sit there day after day, month after month, year after year and listen to debate by insult.
Our experience over the years since 1933 would indicate and should have taught us this thing that is pointed out by so many observers and writers, that, all the way along, the cheapest communist commodity has been talk, as long as the western nations were not prepared to give things away as fast and as freely as the Russians and other communist nations thought we should. The classic example of how quickly these things can be done when the western nations are prepared to give Russia what she wants was the Teheran conference in 1943. At that time Russia, we are told, wanted a second front in Europe, and more lend-lease goods. President Roosevelt agreed to both terms. Russia merely gave a few inconsequential promises and a quick agreement was effected.
Then, any hon. members who have read Mr. Churchill's recent book, "Triumph and Tragedy", will recall that at Yalta in 1945 a very great part of the world was put under the sway of Russia. Mr. Churchill states that he jotted down on a piece of paper a formula for dividing up influence in the Balkan states. He shoved it over quietly to Stalin, who very quickly put some sort of cryptic mark on it, and that is all there was to it. There was no need for long talks under such conditions as those. And Mr. Churchill said that it was all over in no more time than it takes to set it down on paper.

External Affairs
Then six months after Yalta, at the Potsdam conference, the United States agreed to give the Russians just about everything they wanted in eastern Germany, and also agreed to let the Russians haul out of Germany-all parts of it-into Russia, vast quantities of machinery and plants of every description.
Anyone who has taken the trouble to look at the formation of the boundaries between the eastern and western zones of Germany, as I have done, can see how cleverly every single power plant was carved out of the western zone and made to appear in the eastern zone. And when one looks at those things he will understand just how easily the Russians got what they wanted. At Potsdam the Russians really smiled and, we are told, nodded in agreement, said a few words and went home perfectly happy.
Over the past eight years 94 meetings have been held between the western and eastern powers concerning disarmament. Over three million words have been spoken on that subject, but no agreement has been reached, nor does it seem at the present time as though one is in sight.
At the United Nations general assembly, and in the security council, 35 million words have been spoken on widely varying topics- world peace, and the problems the nations face. And in this great world forum the communists have quibbled, they have thumped the tub, and have used every opportunity to proclaim their propaganda. They have denounced the western nations, and they have sometimes walked out. Even when they did stay in they conducted their debate like a bunch of rowdies, resorting almost constantly to debate by insults.
Words, I say, have been communist weapons, the best weapons they have ever used. They have used them not only in a world forum like the United Nations, but they have also used them to take over labour unions and other organizations they wanted to capture. They have used words to take over nations and to win international conferences. Right now there seems to be a period of quiet and peace on what we might call the word front. For some weeks past we have read about the sweetness and joviality and friendliness of the Russian delegates and their friends at the United Nations but we should be warned that behind all this peaceful front there must be the same old communist strategy.
The minister pointed out today how important it was that we take care that we be not divided. Well, we must beware of that, because I am satisfied that the aim of the

communists, in their sweet attitude at the present time, is an effort to divide the free world, with the ultimate hope of course of strengthening their own position so they can dominate the world. As one step toward this effort at division the communists are now bidding for more trade with Europe, the United States and other nations of the world. Well, it seems to me that in over eight years of that sort of thing we should have learned something; I hope we have. For just a few minutes I should like to say something about communism, perhaps in general, and about things we ought to be doing to prevent the communists from achieving their goal of world domination.
When we earnestly seek for a solution to the very great and trying world problems it seems to me that we should adopt a principle to guide us in reaching that decision, out of the experience we have had over the years and realizing as we do how difficult-yes, wellnigh impossible-it is to negotiate with the communists on anything like satisfactory or even terms. We ought to ask ourselves as we approach the problem: will this proposed solution have the effect of strengthening the communist world; or in the alternative, will this proposed solution have the long-range effect of weakening the communist world and consequently of strengthening our own by comparison?
I say we should be guided by the truthful answers to these questions. Certainly I believe that any decision we make should never have the effect of strengthening communism and the communist world, no matter how humanitarian we might wish to be in our outlook and views. If what we are about to do or if what has been proposed will in any way tend to build up communist strength, then I say, Mr. Speaker, we should assiduously avoid that proposal.
We have given too much ground already, in my judgment. Perhaps even in Canada itself it would be well to require of anyone who would dwell in our land that he earn his privileges of citizenship. In the external field I think that rather than welcoming communist dictators and nations with open arms into our fellowship of free nations and giving them every advantage of such fellowship, we should be thinking carefully of modifying the privileges that those countries, especially the U.S.S.R., are enjoying.
I am thinking at the moment of trade. Something was said about it this afternoon by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). He did not say where he stood on the matter. More was said about it by the leader of the C.C.F. party, and he did say where they stood. I am going to say

where I stand. I do not think that the communist nations should be allowed to enjoy the fruits of trade with the western world unless they are prepared to give ample evidence that they value their association with our fellowship and are prepared also to work for the betterment of the world and for its peace and security.
That is a pretty straightforward position,
I would say, and I have reasons for taking that view. There are many people of course who say well, what harm would it do to let the countries of the world sell nonstrategic materials to Russia or to some of the communist nations? I take the view that for the present we should not even be prepared to trade with them in non-strategic materials, because they can use them to increase production of strategic materials and weapons, and that of course would result in building up their strength at the expense of the nations against whom they are constantly working, with the objective of course of destroying us. Why should we send them goods with which they can turn around and cut us down? I do not believe that is sound under any circumstances. There should be no trade even in non-strategic materials between Russia and the fellowship of free nations until, as Mr. Eisenhower said, by deeds and not words they give evidence of a desire to work for peace and for world security, instead of disruption and world domination which seems to be their constant aim.
This of course would look very serious to Britain, because Britain appears to feel that it is necessary for her to trade with China and Russia and perhaps other countries behind the iron curtain. If Great Britain is forced to seek trade behind the iron curtain, as many people seem to think she has been, then nobody is to blame for that situation but the United States, Canada and other parts of the free world. The free world thus far has made trade impossible for Great Britain at a time when all of us should have been doing everything we possibly could to strengthen and to build her up because, Mr. Speaker, Great Britain has been for many years the fount and source of justice, equity, liberty and the rule of law, and to let her be destroyed is nothing less than a world tragedy.
I say again that the free nations of the world by their policies have forced Britain behind the iron curtain, and we have not done what we could to build her up. I was struck with these words in a letter that I received just yesterday from a former member of this house, Mr. Luchkovich, who now lives in the city of Edmonton. I commend
External Affairs
these words to all hon. members. Some of you will remember him when he was here; he was a U.F.A. member. I quote from his letter:
Practising our Canadianism, we must not forget the debt we owe Great Britain. In this struggle we need Great Britain, and Great Britain needs us and our relations with each other must remain intact.
I have no brief for Great Britain by virtue of ties of blood, but I can support her by reason of common sense and national security. Thus I have no desire to twist the lion's tail nor share in the charges of decadency. The British have had the great misfortune of losing the cream and flower of their most able young people in two great world wars. That gap has not as yet been closed. But it will be; and in the meantime they should not have to worry too much so long as they keep on producing Shakespeares, Newtons, Harveys, Watts, Stevensons, Wellingtons and Churchills.
But, being of Ukrainian origin, all I can do is to express my admiration for a people that has maintained its traditions so long, that has stood up so nobly under adversity, that has saved itself by its own efforts, and others by its own example.
The British people have been "running too long with the hounds to be worried by their whelps." They have been the real founders of democracy as it is now understood. Hyde Park is not only a pleasure ground but a safety valve for all the cranks to let off steam. Handsome is as handsome does and names will never hurt the British so long as they do not slough off the white man's burden and discard their role as champion of human and minority rights.
That is the end of the part I wanted to quote. This gentleman of Ukrainian origin rises to the sentiments which should be guiding the whole of the commonwealth today, and we are one of the leading members of the commonwealth.
I said that if Britain has been forced behind the iron curtain to do much of her trading, then nobody can be blamed for that situation but the people of the western world, and we in Canada and the United States must bear our fair share of the blame. What have we done to help to rehabilitate Britain and the commonwealth? What have we done to make Britain's trading easier? What have we done to help that country increase the production of those things which Canada needs and wants from Great Britain?
I am not forgetting that when we were debating the speech from the throne we Social Crediters put forward an idea for trade with Great Britain that I am perfectly satisfied would have been and could now be of tremendous help in bringing that country back to the position which we need her to occupy in this world. I am satisfied that if our proposal at that time that we be prepared to accept some sterling-we did not say "all sterling"-from Britain in the course of our trade to settle some of our balances, that had we been prepared to do so five or six years

External Affairs
ago, I am satisfied that today Britain could be supplying us with many of the things that we need and cannot get there. I am satisfied that if we had started even this year we could have done much in just a few months to help Britain back on her feet; but what was the attitude of hon. members to that proposal? No, sir, they turned it down and said that it would interfere with the determination of the powers that be to retain the dominance and the super-sanctity of the almighty dollar. That was the only reason.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think if we will adopt realistic trade policies we can take care of Great Britain's needs and therefore not force her to trade behind the iron curtain. I believe that under such circumstances we could come nearer to the kind of unity among the countries of the western world that we need. At the present time Great Britain, because she feels the necessity for trade with China, has recognized China, and she advocates that the other free nations of the world recognize her. That is a point of division among the free nations.
Moreover, Great Britain would like to see China become a member of the United Nations largely because of the advantages which might come to her in the world of trade. When the communist world is made to understand that the free flow of trade between their countries and the free nations of the world is a valuable privilege of fellowship that comes only to those worthy of that fellowship, then I am quite certain they will be led to some worth-while introspection and perhaps into a little repentance. I think the most salutary lesson that any human being or group of human beings can learn, that is when he or they have been acting in an anti-social way, is to find some modification of his or their privileges of citizenship or fellowship, whether it is on a national or world scale.
That brings me to the question of communist China's demand for membership in the United Nations. I do not think we should be in any hurry about granting communist China entry into the United Nations. I do not mean to say that eventually she should not have full fellowship there, but what would be her reasons for wanting to become a member now? That is a question that has to be asked. Would it be because she feels she can contribute something to world peace and security? Is she prepared to fulfil and capable of fulfilling her obligations under the terms of the United Nations charter? Or is she anxious to become a member of the United Nations and is Russia
anxious to have her there because she could be a support and a source of strength to the communist world and its disruptive aims by having a seat in the assembly beside the seat of Russia? In his article entitled "Don't Let Asia Split the West" as reprinted from the World of December, 1953, the minister *of external affairs wrote this pungent paragraph:
To understand the meaning of Asian communism, to place It as we should, against the background of foreign exploitation and feudal oppression, is one thing. But it does not mean that at this time we should welcome into the international community, as a state willing to abide by the principles of the United Nations charter, a regime which has committed aggression in Korea and has yet to show that it is willing to contribute to a peaceful and democratic solution of the Korean or other Asian problems.
I am in thorough agreement with those words, and I sincerely hope that Canada will stand by them. In other words, we do not want to exercise any hatred toward Asians as such. They are human beings just the same as we are, and we must be prepared to treat them in every way as equals. As the minister has so well said in other places, "We should unite against aggressors and not against Asians." That is true. But let us say to China, "When you have demonstrated by deeds and not more millions of words that you are willing and prepared to contribute to a peaceful and democratic solution of the Korean and other Asiatic problems; when you are prepared to take your full responsibilities under the terms of the United Nations charter and abide by those terms, then you will be admitted into full fellowship in the United Nations with all the valuable privileges of that fellowship, at least so far as we are concerned."
Mr. Speaker, I have not much more to say and I hope you will turn a blind eye to the clock for just a minute in order that I may complete a point which I wish to make. I am convinced in my own mind, as a matter of fact, that the United Nations would be a much better organization without Russia. There are those who think otherwise and I honour their views, but that is my belief. Russia has never yet contributed anything but frustration and despair and confusion. What hope have we that she will ever contribute anything more in the future? If, of course, she should give evidence of a real change of heart; if she should begin to demonstrate her desire to live up to her responsibilities under the United Nations charter, then of course she should not be denied full fellowship.

I am firmly convinced, however, that the organization would go along much better without Russia and without her satellites so long as they continue their present attitude and practices. We could make far better headway without her. She now uses the organization to spread her propaganda, to get her spies and subversives into this and every other country for one purpose, to undermine and destroy us. I am sure that if Russia did not have full fellowship in the United Nations there would be a much better chance of unity among those nations who are left and who are willing to undertake and discharge their responsibilities under the charter.
If the communist world were denied the privileges of membership in this fellowship of nations, and if we over the years demonstrate that we can make use of it to further and improve our collective and individual security, our standard of living and all of those worth-while things, then I say perhaps Russia and the others might decide that membership is a real privilege for which they should work and for which they should give a real demonstration of their integrity and their willingness to co-operate on a peaceful basis.
I doubt that any other action of the western world short of all-out war will teach the communist aggressors anything of lasting value. I certainly would be the last one to advocate all-out armed conflict. I know what it would mean. My organization and I are committed to strive for international peace and security. We believe that Canada and all other nations should have been striving over the years with all their might to find out what are the real sources of war, and to remove those just as quickly as possible.
We should have been doing everything in our power to remove industrial rivalry among the nations, to establish an equitable distribution of the goods and services this world can produce, and to have them distributed in all nations that are willing to co-operate. We believe that perhaps the greatest single factor leading to international conflict has been the lack of such equitable distribution of the goods and services that were produced. We are unalterably of the opinion that the establishment of sound international trade policies, such as those we have outlined on many occasions, is the best assurance of international peace and security.
At the same time we recognize only too well that there is over the whole face of the world today a conflict of ideologies that is a constant threat to peace and national security. When we realize that this conflict is going on, then we also must be realistic
External Affairs
in recognizing the necessity of organizations such as NATO and the European defence community and that sort of thing. We recognize also the necessity of organizing our own national economy so as to provide good opportunities for economic security for all of our people, along with freedom, so we can help them to be happy and contented in their lot and save them in the struggle that is going on for men's minds.
We hear much about peace and the opportunities for peace. We hon. members are getting letters almost every day from some peace organization. Because we speak sometimes with vigour, because we advocate allout vigilance, some of us are often understood to be belligerent. I hope there will be an intelligent differentiation between the two, as certainly there is a difference. To be vigilant is not to be belligerent. Vigilance is all we want.
Speaking of peace may I say that to us, except life itself and liberty there is probably nothing that we cherish as much as peace. Perhaps more of us do not find it because we do not understand the nature of peace. Today men and nations alike are running to and fro in search of it, some of them hoping to purchase it at a bargain-and I speak of Russia as one-some fully expecting to pay its entire price but not knowing what that price must be.
Perhaps these people have forgotten, or perhaps they never knew, that peace does not depend upon the accumulation of material things, nor upon the accident of chancing to be in one place or another on this globe, but rather that peace comes from an attitude of mind which leaves the windows of the soul open to all truth, and the will to live in accordance with that truth. This every man should know-
