Very well, Mr. Speaker. I have just one sentence to finish. I want to make absolutely certain that every member of this house realizes that there is a price that must be paid for peace, and that we must be willing to pay that price. If we do not realize that, of course we have no basis upon which to seek for peace.

External Affairs
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say we should know that peace may be found by earnest searchers for it, and certainly not by restless journeys over the world from this country to behind the iron curtain where you can learn methods of subversion. I hope we shall make it impossible in the future for some of our so-called world citizens and fellow travellers to make such easy trips behind the iron curtain to learn the art of peace that they want to buy at an easy price.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roch Pinard (Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although on past occasions I have had the opportunity of discussing matters concerning international affairs, this is the first chance I have had to do so as parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I am indeed grateful to him for this opportunity which he has given me to express certain views on this important subject.
As he suggested this afternoon, I shall deal briefly with the activities of the United Nations at the last session of the general assembly last fall. As I had occasion to attend only the latter part of that session, I must say that I had to depend upon the assistance and co-operation of the members of the Canadian delegation in order to form an opinion as to what was going on. Afterward I could follow with ease the developments that were taking place.
While Korean developments outside the United Nations itself held the spotlight of public attention, the general assembly concerned itself during its eighth session with other matters reflecting a vast range of problems of concern to the international community. The eighth session was shorter than preceding sessions. In fact it began in mid-September and lasted only until the early part of December. In spite of that fact, the agenda was quite lengthy and in every field -political, economic, social, administrative and legal

there were issues pressing for solution. The delegations applied themselves to the work of the various committees in a businesslike manner under the guidance of the chairmen of the committees, including our own Dr. George Davidson, who acted with great competence as chairman of the social committee. The various delegations carried on the work at a good pace.
Glancing back at the eighth session of the assembly, one cannot be aware of much in the way of really constructive achievement. Nonetheless there is evidence of a generally high level of progress on the varied questions with which the assembly was concerned. This session was something of a transitional one, 
spanning the period between the termination of the Korean conflict and the post-Korea relationships that may develop in its wake. The assembly made some progress on problems of long standing, but did not advance far on issues on which there remained, as usual, a major clash of interest.
The atmosphere of the assembly was influenced, as it generally is, by the current international climate, and particularly by the fact that some of the major problems, such as the Korea problem and the prospect of a meeting of the big four powers on Germany, were being dealt with elsewhere. Nevertheless the United Nations continued to provide a valuable meeting ground for east and west, and it kept in motion in the right direction the machinery of international co-operation.
At the beginning of the session our Secretary of State for External Affairs had to resume his function as head of the Canadian delegation after he turned over to his successor, Madame Pandit of India, the duties of president of the general assembly. I think I express a view which is shared by most members of this house when I say that our country was extremely proud to have as one of its most distinguished sons one who did such a wonderful job as president of that important international body. His sense of duty and the effective way in which he conducted the proceedings gave to the people of Canada another reason to believe that our Secretary of State for External Affairs enjoys the reputation of being not only a great diplomat but a really great Canadian.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss in my duty were I not to congratulate the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) who was acting president of the eighth session of the general assembly during the long absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). The Postmaster General discharged these duties with ability while losing nothing of his usual geniality.
I would also like to point out the excellent work done by my colleague from Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) who also happens to be my member, since I have the honour of living in his constituency. He was an assiduous participant in all discussions, as a delegate, more particularly in the legal committee to which he brought his long experience in the field of law.
(Text):
In the work of the Canadian delegation, Mr. Speaker, we were also assisted by the presence of parliamentary observers from each of the main parties represented in this house;

and I feel sure that this arrangement, which is based upon the practice followed in earlier years, has fully justified itself.
As in previous sessions, several major problems which are not new played a large part in assembly discussions and will, I am afraid, continue in the future to challenge our collective resources of intelligence and good will. These arose from issues of nationalism, colonialism and racialism. We have witnessed in acute form the practical problems which arise in this world organization in seeking to reconcile the principle of the domestic jurisdiction of sovereign states over dependent peoples with the legitimate interest of the United Nations in human rights and peaceful progress towards a wider freedom for all peoples. These are not merely arid, constitutional debates. They relate to issues which, in a dynamic world, arouse strong passions and directly concern the fate of many millions of human beings.
For the most part these problems have been considered in a spirit of moderation. These great issues cannot be determined by a rigid and formal reference to the letter of the charter. I would think that the charter of the United Nations could be compared in some ways with the constitution of a nation. A constitution must have some flexibility, and must never become the master but should always remain the servant of the people. The same thing, I think, should apply to the charter of the United Nations, so that on occasion amendments should be brought forward in order to have a charter that will suit in a better way the general interests of this organization.
It must be recognized that the force of nationalism, to which I was referring, and the urge for independence are among the strongest and most explosive elements in the world today. In seeking to direct these forces toward the path of order and non-violence the United Nations has one of its most important roles to play. Such problems arose in the case of the items dealing with Morocco and Tunisia, to which the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) referred this afternoon, and other problems relating to the development of self-government and charges of racial discrimination were also discussed.
Here delegations faced alternatives not easy to resolve or reconcile. Here were problems on which the Asian and Arab states feel particularly strongly, because to them the rights and wrongs of the case are so clearly defined. Because of this they perhaps found it difficult to understand why, in the voting in the general assembly, the Canadian delegation was not able to be always
External Affairs
fully on their side, and at times had to oppose them. The basic reason for this is, I think, the difference of emphasis which we on the one hand, and the Arab-Asian states, on the other, place on the many factors which enter into the problem. We in the western world and the Arab and Asian states are in principle united on basic aims. It is on the choice of the best means to achieve them that we sometimes differ.
The Canadian people know too well the price to be attached to freedom of government not to be in accord with other countries which are now striving towards the same end. As citizens of a country which has gradually and peacefully transformed its status from that of a simple colony to that of a free nation, it is our duty to look with sympathy upon problems of the same nature which are facing other peoples who are also trying to attain maturity and independence. But we also have our duty to perform according to the terms of the charter of the United Nations. Our intervention in matters of that kind must not be of a kind which would endanger the peaceful relations of people in those areas.
At each session of the United Nations we also look anxiously for concrete actions which will provide a test of the real intentions of the Soviet union and of the sincerity of the desire of Soviet leaders to reduce international tensions. With the best will in the world, it cannot be said that the eighth session has been marked by any basic change in Soviet actions. The house will be well aware of the difficulties in getting the political conference started in Korea. In other fields Soviet spokesmen and their satellites have persisted in their traditional positions as, for example, on the disarmament issue; or have continued to use the assembly as a platform for their usual propaganda lines, as in colonial questions or on the issue of charter revision.
The Soviet delegation insisted in putting on the agenda near the end of the session an item on international tension. But the way to reduce international tension is not to talk about it; it is to tackle, in a spirit of co-operation, the practical difficulties and current problems which face us. There is as yet no concrete evidence that the Soviet union is willing to act in this way.
This was especially true on the question of disarmament. When this matter was debated in plenary meeting last spring the co-operative attitude adopted by Mr. Vishinsky caused many of us to think that possibly the Soviet union had begun to think

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Today, for the first time during the present session, Mr. Speaker, as well as for the first time in the year 1954, a day has been set aside for the discussion of our survival. We are not talking about external affairs or the interests of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). We are talking about the hope of civilization for survival. I trust that the interest in survival is greater than might at some moments appear to be the case.
I have a sense of a feeling of unreality concerning the things that have been said, and the way in which the very ominous picture before us today has been analysed. In some ways I cannot help but feel that this is where some of us came in. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) brings back to my mind memories that are associated with the nature of the discussion today. I mention him because I have known him longer than any other member in this house except the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson). I played football with the member for Vancouver South many years ago. I played football with the member for Simcoe North still earlier.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
You were a wonderful
kicker even then.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
I remember that at that time I
was doing the kicking and helping on the half line of the team at the University of Toronto. I was centre half. The right half was the son of a very well known Liberal, who was presumed to be Liberal himself. The left half was rather regarded as a left, but we were all good friends. I presume I was wrong in the assessment that was placed on his views at that time, but as I have said we were all good friends. It does not seem so long ago, unfortunately, and then it was not very long after that until we found ourselves in the same artillery brigade overseas.
I only mention that now because it brings back to my memory many of the pleasures of life in the days before the first world war; and it was a very pleasant life. It also brings back to my memory a different kind of war, a stern war, a war which we were then led to believe was a war to end war. It was, in fact, Armageddon.
It did not turn out that way. When the war was over, following the armistice signed on November 11, 1918-which	significantly
enough we still remember rather than the date named as the day of peace-we had dreams of a new and sensible world, where reason was going to prevail. Young men of that time, like the hon. member for Vancouver South, myself and others, many of them now

External Affairs
in this house, having regard to the lessons of the days before the war, thought that the league of nations which was then created under a charter which was part of the treaty of Versailles had in fact set up a brave new world where the joint common sense of men and women was going to prevent a repetition of that horror which most of us had seen.
That horror was seen and shared by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) just as it was by others who are here today. The dream was not entirely visionary but the dream broke down. The dream became nothing but a dream and it became nothing but a dream because those who had created this bright vision had not been able to sufficiently impress upon those who followed them the simple and inescapable fact that words and platitudes are never a substitute for that type of joint action which would prevent aggression just in the same way that you prevent, within some reasonable measure, the complete breakdown of society within the many organized communities of the world.
Then came the last world war, a war that everyone agreed in 1939 and 1940 had actually been brought closer and closer to certainty by the appeasement which encouraged the aggressor to move one step farther every time the last step succeeded beyond his highest hopes. Look back at the newspapers of 1939 and 1940, and see how everyone who was called upon to speak at every important public forum was saying that never again would the word "appeasement" be written across the face of the world in letters of blood. That was the lesson that we said we had learned.
With that impression in the minds of men and women, and with all the limitless horrors of the last world war still fresh in their minds, representatives of most of the nations of the world gathered at San Francisco in the spring of 1945 and signed the charter of the United Nations, with the hope that the failure of the league of nations would warn them of the danger of forgetting some of the lessons of days gone by.
Who can forget the warnings of that great statesman, Jan Christiaan Smuts, the man who actually first conceived the form of the league of nations. His was the warning that if this was to become a reality, then everyone should remember that the way to peace was not to be found along the road of appeasement. And there were others there with similar memories. I think the time has come for every one of us to urge that in the name of decency and civilization we should revive

those memories, and remember that when we emphasized the dangers of appeasement it was simply with the thought of seeking to emphasize the danger of war itself.
Today we have heard external affairs discussed. I would be less than frank if I said tonight that I thought the Secretary of State for External Affairs had told us anything about external affairs, other than to repeat things that we already knew, except as to the decision of the government in regard to the invitation of India for a reconvening of the United Nations. I may have missed something, but I cannot recall a single thing he told us that was not already a matter of common knowledge. And this is the first debate we have had on external affairs. If I am wrong in what I have said I would be glad to be corrected.
As the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said today when speaking on behalf of this party, we want as much agreement as there possibly can be in regard to external affairs. To whatever extent that is possible, we want a single policy which will represent the people of Canada. Mr. Speaker, a policy of that kind can come only when external affairs are discussed in an atmosphere of reality, and when the spirit and faith and belief of the members are challenged by the feeling that we are being taken into the confidence of the government, publicly, so far as possible, and privately to whatever extent that can be justified.
Passing from the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I want to speak about certain statements that were made this afternoon by the leader of the C.C.F. party. He spoke about the immense change that has taken place in Russia within these past few months. They have; tremendous changes have taken place. Stalin died less than a year ago. At that time there was great speculation whether his successor would be Beria or Malenkov. Malenkov was the successor. The leader of the opposition and his associates were disposed of; they have a somewhat different system there.
This was no removal of some disturbing element in the country. He was disturbing only to the extent that, conceivably, he might have challenged Malenkov's position. Of course, as has been pointed out already, his was the usual fate of those who have occupied the same post. I cannot recall a single head of the secret police in Russia since the revolution who has not been disposed of in the same way. I do not know why it is still possible to fill that office.
But surely anybody must be almost
unbelievably naive who thinks that Malenkov was suddenly imbued with some high

moral purpose which led him to dispose of this fiend who had murdered many people in Russia over the years. Of course he had; but that is the business of any man in that job in Russia, and it will be the business of the man who is in that job in Russia now. And it was the business of the men who did that job, when they removed Beria and his associates, as they have removed many others. Yes, there have been changes. A new ruler exercises that unlimited power. Oh, yes, there are different appearances. The gestures of friendship have been made. Well, surely our memories are not so short that we do not remember the same gestures of friendship in the years just before the last world war.
It happens that I was in Moscow at the time they were carrying out a similar political change some years ago, in fact, at the time they were disposing of Tukachevski and Yakir and a number of other Russian generals in 1937. History is simply repeating itself. At that time visitors to Russia were welcomed more than they have been since the last war. The gestures of friendship on the surface were there. It was possible to find many pleasant things; art, music-all were to be found in Moscow or Leningrad in the buildings that had been erected long before the revolution. There were pleasant things there, pleasant and deceptive things.
No, the picture has not greatly changed. But then I was struck by the words of the leader of the C.C.F. when he said we may be entering a period of peaceful negotiation. Let us not forget the Russian willingness to negotiate; let us not forget the readiness of the Russians to negotiate with nazi Germany in 1939. Let us not forget that if the Russian government had not signed an agreement with nazi Germany on August 26, 1939, while they were actually negotiating with the British and the French at the same time in Moscow, it is still uncertain whether Hitler would have dared to move at that time. They were still in advance of their schedule. Do not let anybody forget the pictures they can see in the press if they are not still clear in their minds, of Mr. Molotov, who is now in Berlin, side by side with von Ribbentrop signing that agreement in the Kremlin when they pledged themselves in a friendship that was to be everlasting.
Yes, they negotiate; they will sign anything, and the documents that have been disclosed since the war make it perfectly clear that when they signed that agreement on August 26, 1939, they had no more sincerity of purpose than had the Germans. Both of them were planning for what was going to take place at the next stage.
External Affairs
It was not many days after that when Germany struck in that unprovoked attack on Poland which brought the free nations into the last war. It was not because any inch of the soil of Britain, of France, of any part of the British commonwealth or of the United States was challenged at that time. It was because a great principle was challenged, and that was the right of nations to live their own lives and not be subject to unprovoked aggression such as nazi Germany committed in the attack. And then what happened? Did Russia repudiate the agreement and become indignant at this breach of the understanding? No; they went in for their share. Greatly to the distaste of the Germans they moved in and occupied the other half of Poland. When thieves fall out trouble really begins. One of the thieves has been dealt with; the other is now prepared to negotiate once again.
I am repeating only in capsule form the tragic history of those early days of the last war that we should not forget. When we talk about negotiation let us remember that those are the same people-that is, those of them who have survived-and their manner of doing business has not changed in any way.
I was disturbed, and greatly disturbed, by the remarks made by the leader of the C.C.F. party in regard to the possible establishment of Soviet bases in certain parts of the world. I was disturbed because I recognize without any reservation his complete sincerity in his approach to this problem. I was disturbed because I recognized his sincerity and the extent to which many people appear to forget some of the events of even the most recent years. He said:	"I wonder what we would
think if the Soviet union sought to establish bases in Cuba or in Mexico?" He asked us to think of how this would be regarded in the United States as an evident sign of aggression. He may not have intended it, but I almost heard the speech I heard Bevan make in the House of Commons in Britain when he pictured two aggressors between whom there was not very much of a choice. I hope this is not the interpretation to be placed upon those remarks; but let us take what he said: "What would we think if we found the Soviet seeking to establish bases in Mexico or in Cuba or in those other places?"
Let us remember, Mr. Speaker, that the Soviets have sought to establish bases in other places throughout the world where they could get bases, and they have been very successful. Who brought the Soviet troops into East Germany? Who brought the Soviet troops into Czechoslovakia? Who brought the Soviet troops into all of eastern

External Affairs
Europe? Then let us go back in our memory to Spain, in the days before the last war. Did I hear someone say "Churchill"? Anyone who said "Churchill" is unworthy to sit in this house, if he was suggesting that Churchill was responsible for their going in there.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: I was the one who said "Churchill" and my comment was that Churchill was the one who negotiated with the Russians.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
I was speaking of Spain, and the hon. member knew I was speaking of Spain. I have heard that same statement before. Now, let us be quite clear that no one saw more clearly than Churchill did what was happening in Spain. Read his speeches of that time, and let no one here suggest that Churchill did not see before the last war as clearly as any human being in the world what was happening in that area, as in other parts where the bitter signs of war were still not apparent to some who sought peace just as much as he did.
No, let us not forget the friendship of Franco for those who were opposed to the things for which we stand. But let us not forget that what brought Franco to power in Spain was the communist government under Caballero. Do not let anybody suggest that it was not a communist government.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: Do not let anybody suggest that it was not a communist government. I saw in Moscow tribute being paid to representatives of the people who had put Caballero there, and who were being honoured by the communists in Moscow at that time.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Does the hon.
member deny that it was the fascist and the nazi brigades that finally put Franco in power?

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
I know my history too well not to know perfectly well who brought Franco to power. What brought Franco to power was exactly the same thing that brought Hitler to power in Germany and Mussolini to power in Italy. It was the communists; and the people who were determined to drive out communism went to another dangerous extreme. In every case these vile dictatorships have been the spawn of communism itself. Do not let anyone to my left or elsewhere distort history today. It was the vile abuses of the communist-supported and communist government of Caballero that were condemned by Churchill and by those who knew what was taking place. But do you suppose for one minute that if Caballero had stayed there, Russia would not have continued to supply Caballero with the guns,

the tanks and the weapons that they had been supplying him with? Certainly weapons were supplied on the other side, and unhappily the first round of the last world war was in some measure fought in Spain. Every one of us knows that the fascists of Italy and the nazis of Germany took one side, with the communists on the other. But do not let anyone suggest that Russia has not been willing to establish bases wherever she could.
Do not think for one moment that if Russia had succeeded in gaining control of Italy through their regime there under Togliatti they would not have supplied Italy with arms, weapons and the supplies of war today. Do not believe for one moment that if they had succeeded in their dream, in which thank God they failed, of imposing a communist government on France under Thorez they would not have supplied them with guns and tanks and weapons, and that we would have been facing a very much more dreadful picture than we do today.
No, let us not get this picture distorted in any way. The suggestion that the Russians have reason to be alarmed about the establishment of bases by the United States in different parts of the world denies one very simple fact. Russia has been the great aggressor since the last war, and has brought more human beings under that vile dictatorship than were ever brought under slavery in the same period of time in the long history of the world. In that same time not one act of aggression of any kind could be charged to the government of the United States which, thank God, is our ally in this great cause. That is something to remember.
Do not suggest that those two things are on the same basis. I was disturbed today when I heard the suggestion that the NATO forces were capable of stemming aggression. We know they are not. We know that they are not in position to stem the forces of Russia assembled in Europe today. We do know that with the immense bombing power of the United States and Britain those forces can be effective to prevent aggression; but the compelling deterrent, and never let us forget it, at this time is the immense bombing power of the United States and Britain. I repeat, "and Britain". Let us pass from that.
I have dealt with these things because it would be very unfortunate if in seeking peace we forgot any of the recent lessons of history, or were beguiled into any belief that the peaceful front presented under the new leader in the Kremlin offers any assurance of good intentions until some evidence of good

intention, which has not yet been given, is offered as evidence to the world of any substantial change.
Mr. Speaker, we have heard today of the horrors of another war. I do not think anyone needs to be reminded of that. Anyone who follows the radio and reads the press knows perfectly well the unbelievable extension of the deadly power of nuclear weapons. But let us always recall that the increase in the deadliness of weapons does not change a single principle which we accepted under the charter of the United Nations at San Francisco or a single lesson we were supposed to have learned in the years between the two world wars and the ghastly tragedy that followed.
In the last few days we may well have reached a dramatic turning point in history. No one can yet say with finality what is going to emerge from the conference in Berlin. Let us see quite clearly what did emerge from the proposal made on behalf of Russia by Mr. Molotov at the beginning of that conference. He proposed that China be seated immediately as one of the big five. He went further, however, and indicated quite clearly that if this proposal were accepted, then the western powers could count on the good offices of Russia to bring about peace in Korea and Indo-China.
Mr. Speaker, whatever was intended by that statement, one thing emerged in unmistakable form. How can Russia again deny their full authority over China? How can Russia again deny that they are in a position to pull the strings? That was their bait. That was their promise. They said if we accepted communist China as one of the big five they would do what we have all said Russia1 could do.
That did something more. It centred international diplomacy on the willingness or otherwise of the free nations to recognize communist China, to give such further recognition and to be prepared to accept her in the United Nations. It meant nothing else. They are to be one of the big five. That means they are to be one of the five permanent members of the United Nations security council. It had no other meaning and was not intended to have any other meaning.
It is granted that certain other things have happened since then; but I think most of us will be greatly surprised if this conference ends with that position changed. I think most of us will be surprised if this conference does not end with the Russian demand still there, that the price of negotiation, the
External Affairs
price of peace which they can enforce upon their puppets, is the recognition of communist China and the entry of communist China into the United Nations. They were called to Berlin to talk about the unification of Germany and Austria, but the focal point of international diplomacy has been carried across two oceans and this continent to China.
Mr. Speaker, all the members of this house may not have agreed from time to time with the things that have been said by Mr. Dulles. However, it may be a good thing at this time that issues are presented not in the old terms of veiled diplomacy but in direct and understandable words that ordinary human beings throughout the world can really understand. Mr. Dulles used words of that kind the day before yesterday. This is what he said:
"But who is this Chou En-lai?" Dulles asked. "He is the leader of a regime which attained de facto power through bloody war, which liquidated millions of Chinese as the only means of maintaining power and which devotes so much of its resources to military aims that its people starve by the millions. Such is the man who, Mr. Molotov says, should sit with us. Mr. Molotov has portrayed an illusion. Our moral sense forbids us to accept him."
I hope that in this house we will say that our moral sense forbids us to accept Chou En-lai, Mao Tse-tung or any of the communist hierarchy who are murdering their countrymen in the name of communism in China today. As to the Asian communists, we hear them spoken of as though this were a denatured form of communism. Perhaps it would be well for us not to forget that a substantial part of Russia is in Asia. That fact, of course, gave them the opportunity to train, equip, finance and feed their fifth column under Mao which they organized on the borders of Russia until it was ready to invade China. Do not let anyone pretend that this was an agrarian uprising or an expression of new social consciousness of the people of China. Do not let anybody suggest that this was a Chinese revolt. It was an invasion by a Chinese communist fifth column led by Mao and under the direction of Moscow at all times, as it still is today. If we had been in any doubt about that fact, Mr. Molotov has made it plain by saying that if that puppet government is recognized and accepted in the United Nations, he will use his power to bring peace in Asia.
No, this is not some new expression of Chinese social consciousness. Neither I nor, I hope, anyone else here would suggest that conditions in China were admirable under the government which preceded the present government there, but one of the things

External Affairs
which seems at times to be difficult to comprehend is the way in which Chiang Kai-shek suddenly became the human incarnation of evil the moment that Russian military power happened to be able to move Mao in to form a new government in Peking.
No, Chiang Kai-shek was not giving China democratic government, nor had it ever had democratic government. But let us be quite sure that China will never have democratic government under the present government there. Let us not shed any crocodile tears for the man who has succeeded Chiang Kai-shek, even if one is able suddenly to forget that not so long ago we did find it possible to express some admiration for Chiang Kai-shek because of the fortitude which was shown for many years in stemming Japanese aggression while the rest of the world was twiddling its thumbs and letting aggression take its course. Have we forgotten the report on Japanese aggression prepared by a commission of which a great Canadian jurist formed a part? Have we forgotten what we were told at that time about the possibility of stemming Japanese aggression? I hope not. But we seem to have forgotten that at that time, whatever his methods of government may have been, Chiang Kai-shek was able to lead the Chinese people in resistance to that aggression for a long time.
It was because of his long struggle against a common enemy at that time that China became one of the big five, not because it happened to occupy a particular part of the map of Asia or because of any particular tradition or background. China, under Chiang Kai-shek, became one of the big five because they had fought aggression longer than had any other nation at that time. That is something to be remembered when, too lightly, any suggestion may be made that Mao should step into Chiang's position and assume the same dignity and authority that was accorded to China at that time because of what they had done to fight aggression.
We have many Chinese in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and I have yet to meet a Chinaman in Canada who supports the present communist government in that country-not one, and I have met many of them. I do not think those who live in Vancouver will find many Chinese in Chinatown who will express any support, veiled or otherwise, of the communist government in Peking. I think that is true right across this country. It has certainly been true any place where I have met the many Chinese I have met in these past few years since the communist fifth column under Mao invaded China. No, the Chinese in this country dream of that day

when this ghastly slavery will be ended and when, halting though the steps may be, once again the forward march of the Chinese people toward something of our kind of democracy may begin.
That brings us to the age-old question which applies not only in China but elsewhere. Am I my brother's keeper? I must confess some surprise that there are those who seem to be ready to accept the existence of communist governments imposed by force or threat of force as the status quo, but who are satisfied simply to bask in the sunshine of our own freedom and offer no hope of sunshine or light to those people now living in the darkness of communist slavery. I hope no one will interpret what I have said as suggesting that we can or should contemplate, or would under any conceivable circumstances think of contemplating, a military movement against the governments of any of these countries. No sensible person would even contemplate that possibility. But the least we can do is to stand firm in our own convictions and, standing firm in our own convictions, insist that Russia, which signed the charter of the United Nations in the spring of 1945, extend to those nations outside of Russia which are now enslaved and are servants of the Kremlin an opportunity to choose by a free vote their own form of government.
Is that a vague and unreasonable ideal? It is only a vague and unreasonable ideal if we did an utterly unreasonable thing in 1939 when we regarded the invasion of Poland as a challenge to the fundamental principle that every nation has a right to choose its own form of government, whether it be communist or otherwise, as long as it is their own choice. Are we going to forget the millions of people of Poland who did, for a while, have hope? Are we going to forget the millions of people of the Ukraine who, for a while, also had hope and were free?
May I interject at this point that I hope no one will suggest that the Ukraine is part of Russia. If it is, the representative of the Ukraine has no right to be sitting as a representative of an independent nation at the United Nations in New York now.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: He has no right anyway.

subsubtopic: SURVEY OP WORLD AFFAIRS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
In any event, Russia itself is one country that cannot deny that the Ukraine is an independent country, because they insisted that the Ukraine be recognized as an independent country and that their representative be seated there in that capacity. No; in this case we can claim Russian support for the proposition that the Ukraine is an independent country, and I

hope the time will come when that support may be extremely valuable to the people of the Ukraine and all who love freedom.
Have we forgotten the people of Czechoslovakia who, before the last war, had one of the finest democracies to be found anywhere in the world, a peaceful, peace-loving, vigorous, dynamic democracy, betrayed by communists who unhappily were brought into the government of that country in the mistaken idea that you can deal with communists? Have we forgotten the people of Hungary? Remember, Hungary is no stranger to democracy. The golden bull which declared the freedom of the people of Hungary was signed a few years before Magna Carta. That lovely parliament building on the bank of the Danube was one of the great homes of democracy in the world.
Have we forgotten the people of Bulgaria? No, I am not going to suggest that they understood the processes of democracy, but they had their form of government which was their own, and they are now under Russian control. Have we forgotten the people of Roumania, an enlightened country with a great culture and great traditions? Have we forgotten Lithuania on the Baltic, Latvia and Estonia where, before this last war, people were living in decency, comfort and democracy which was a beautiful and shining contrast to the life in Russia to the south of them? Have we forgotten the people in other parts of the world, including China, who have been brought under this slavery? I hope not.
At the moment all we can hope to do is to stand firm in our own convictions. But there is one way that we can test the good faith of Russia which does not depend upon negotiations, and it seems to me such a simple test. Let us simply place before them the charter of the United Nations, and remind them of their signature to that charter. Then we could recall to them certain provisions of that charter, and recall that in the preamble to the charter itself there was the assertion, supported by Russia as one of the big five, that every nation is equal in its right to determine its own course. Russia has brought hundreds of millions of people under as vile a form of slavery as the world has ever seen in these years since the last world war. Can anyone suggest that, if Russia were seeking entry to the United Nations today, any person who had been even moderately informed on modern history could support Russia's entry without repudiating every sanction of the United Nations itself?
Now, having said that, I recognize that Russia is a member. There are provisions
External Affairs
for expulsion. I recognize that it would be folly, that it would be meaningless, to discuss the expulsion of Russia. She is one of the big five with veto power in the security council, so we would not get very far with that. But, Mr. Speaker, China with its puppet government is an aggressor, so declared by the United Nations in Korea, and still an active aggressor in Indo-China today. I fail to see how anyone who retains any mental integrity in their approach to the undertakings of the United Nations can suggest that, under present conditions, China could even be considered for membership in the United Nations.
Let us remember, of course, the distinction between recognition and entry into the United Nations. There seems to be confusion about that. Recognition simply means formal recognition of a government as the de facto government of the state with which we are prepared to do business. Whether or not we are prepared to do business with communist China is something still to be considered, but there is a vast difference between recognition and the entry of the government of communist China into the United Nations. What a travesty it would be if we even discussed it while countries like Portugal, Italy, Japan, West Germany, Austria, Finland, Switzerland and Spain, which we have recognized and to which we send diplomatic representatives, are not members of that organization. What a travesty it would be if we found the dictatorship of Salazar so offensive that we could not admit Portugal, our friend for so long in peace and war, and at the same time we would contemplate the entry of the government of communist China, whose hands are dripping with the blood of the people they have murdered in their rise to power.
No, Mr. Speaker, there could be too high a price to pay. In saying that, I am not suggesting for one moment that we should contemplate the possibility of the kind of terror that would be visited on the world in a modern atomic war. Let me repeat that if we meant what we said back in 1939-40, then we believed at that time-and we might have reason to believe today-that appeasement leads to war, and that the way to preserve peace is to stand firm in a common cause, not to temporize with those who have betrayed every decent undertaking to which they subscribed at a time when we were associated with them in an effort to prevent aggression during the last world war.
No, Mr. Speaker; let us have more reality in discussing this subject. Let us ask that Russia give us evidence of her good faith

External Affairs
before we proceed with further negotiations. I repeat that evidence of good faith can easily be offered, simply by agreeing to permit a free vote in one of those countries I have mentioned as a first step toward honouring their signature to the charter of the United Nations. Let them pick Poland, the Ukraine, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Roumania, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, China or any other country which they have occupied, including Tibet; let them display a single bit of evidence of good faith in that way. Otherwise we are simply following the age-old course to ruin.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, one of the most dramatic pictures in the Scriptures is that of the devil conveying the Saviour to a high place and offering him all the realms of the world in return for a bond under which the position of the devil would be recognized. Throughout history not only the Christians but all those who believe in the same principle have followed that example of salvation by repudiating any bargain of that kind. The road to salvation is found along other ways, not along the road to appeasement or bargains of that nature. We want peace by every device within human power. Let us prevent this supreme catastrophe but, Mr. Speaker, let our voices be raised in a way that will leave no doubt that in Canada we want no bargain with the devil.
